title: Croley-Evans Site
summary: In Knox County, the Croley-Evans site holds a Mississippian town with a platform mound, studied by University of Kentucky archaeologists in 1996.
bodyMarkdown:
The Croley-Evans site (15KX24) is the remains of a Mississippian town with a platform mound in Knox County. People lived there for centuries before European contact. It is one of the few sites in southeastern Kentucky where an early colonial explorer and modern archaeologists described the same place.

## A Mississippian town

The [Mississippian culture](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mississippian_culture) was a way of life built on maize farming, platform mounds and towns tied into wide exchange networks. Croley-Evans belonged to that world.

A 1996 study by University of Kentucky archaeologist Richard Jefferies and colleagues, [“Mississippian adaptation on the northern periphery,”](https://scholars.uky.edu/en/publications/mississippian-adaptation-on-the-northern-periphery-settlement-sub/) calls the site a town-and-mound complex. Radiocarbon dates place its most intensive Mississippian occupation from about A.D. 1200 to 1450.

The authors find that Upper Cumberland groups shared many traits with "mainstream" Mississippian peoples to the south and west. But they expressed those traits in ways that reflect the region's position on the edge of the Mississippian Southeast.

## Excavation

Jefferies excavated the site in the summers of 1993 and 1994. Charles Mayer Dupier Jr., who took part in the 1993 work, described it in a [2000 Filson Club History Quarterly article on prehistoric trails](https://npshistory.com/publications/cuga/fchq-v74n4-2000.pdf) as a Mississippian town with a platform mound and a habitation area of about five hectares, roughly twelve acres.

A 2000 report on the site's Area 2, listed in the [Digital Archaeological Record](https://core.tdar.org/document/206215/archaeological-investigations-at-area-2-of-the-croley-evans-site-a-mississippian-mound-center-in-southeastern-kentucky), records a University of Kentucky field school. Its subject terms include pottery, chipped stone, shell, a shell gorget and human burial.

## What Thomas Walker saw

In April 1750, explorer [Thomas Walker](/stories/thomas-walker-and-cumberland-gap/) passed through the area on his survey for the Loyal Land Company. Dupier quotes Walker's journal describing "the remains of several Indian cabbins and amongst them a round Hill made by Art about 20 feet high and 60 over the Top."

Dupier identifies this as a description of Croley-Evans. He argues that a town of this size likely sat on trails linking it to other settlements. Walker may have followed one of those Native paths.

## Kentucky today

Croley-Evans was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1985 for its information potential. The [NPGallery record](https://npgallery.nps.gov/AssetDetail/NRIS/85002975) lists its address as restricted. The site's buried houses, burials and artifacts are a record of the Mississippian people of the upper Cumberland, best left undisturbed.
